facts.statement: Malawania was an extinct basal thunnosaurian ichthyosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous in what is now Iraq.
facts.quote: Malawania is an extinct genus of basal thunnosaurian ichthyosaur that lived during the Hauterivian or Barremian stages of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Iraq.

facts.statement: Malawania is nicknamed the "out-of-time swimmer" because its primitive anatomy contrasts sharply with its Early Cretaceous age.
facts.quote: Its scientific name, meaning "out-of-time swimmer", refers to the taxon's seemingly anachronistic nature, as its primitive anatomy contrasts markedly with its Early Cretaceous age.

facts.statement: The only known specimen of Malawania was discovered in 1952 in Iraqi Kurdistan by a team of British petroleum geologists led by Douglas M. Morton.
facts.quote: The holotype and only currently known specimen of Malawania was discovered in 1952 at Chia Gara, Amadia in Iraqi Kurdistan, by a team of British petroleum geologists led by Douglas M. Morton.

facts.statement: The specimen was donated to the Natural History Museum, London, in 1959 and catalogued as NHMUK PV R6682.
facts.quote: Morton's team transported the specimen to the United Kingdom and donated it to the Natural History Museum, London, in 1959, where it has since been catalogued as NHMUK PV R6682.

facts.statement: The specimen was formally described as the new species Malawania anachronus in 2013 by Valentin Fischer and colleagues.
facts.quote: In a study published in 2013 and led by the Belgian palaeontologist Valentin Fischer, the specimen was designated as the holotype of the new genus and species Malawania anachronus.

facts.statement: The eyeballs of Malawania were supported by scleral rings made of 13 bones.
facts.quote: The eyeballs were supported by rings of 13 bones, known as scleral rings.

facts.statement: The neural spines at the front of Malawania have unique trapezoidal tops.
facts.quote: The well-spaced neural spines towards the front of the animal have trapezoidal tops, a unique feature of this genus.

facts.statement: Malawania has unusually short, trapezoid-shaped humeri, a feature unique to this genus.
facts.quote: The trapezoid-shaped humeri (upper arm bones) are unusually short, a morphology unique to this genus.

facts.statement: The upper end of each humerus in Malawania bears a unique backwards-pointing capitular process.
facts.quote: The upper end of each humerus bears a backwards-pointing projection known as a capitular process. This trait is also unique to Malawania, with the processes of other ichthyosaurs being semicircular.

facts.statement: The lower ends of the humeri in Malawania do not broaden significantly and articulate with the radius and ulna.
facts.quote: The lower ends of the humeri do not broaden significantly, each articulating with two bones, the radius and ulna.

facts.statement: Malawania had four digits in its foreflippers, with two originating from each intermedium bone.
facts.quote: Two digits originate from each intermedium, similar to Ichthyosaurus. There are two other digits in the foreflippers of Malawania for a total of four.

facts.statement: The first digit of Malawania would have had more than nine phalanges when complete, with the first bearing a notch.
facts.quote: The first digit would have had more than nine phalanges (digit bones) when complete, the first of these bearing a notch.

facts.statement: Malawania is classified as a basal thunnosaurian ichthyosaur and is considered a sister taxon to Ichthyosaurus within Ichthyosauridae.
facts.quote: Morphologically, Malawania closely resembles the emblematic Early Jurassic ichthyosaur Ichthyosaurus, with most phylogenetic analyses recovering the two genera as sister taxa within Ichthyosauridae.

facts.statement: Malawania is recognized as the first non-ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaur known to have survived past the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary, approximately 66 million years after the group was previously thought to have gone extinct.
facts.quote: As ichthyosaurids had previously been regarded as having become extinct during the Early Jurassic, approximately 66 million years before the estimated age of Malawania, the latter became the first recognised non-ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaur to have survived beyond the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary.

facts.statement: A 2017 study by Lomax and colleagues recovered Malawania as a basal thunnosaur with Ichthyosaurus as the sister taxon of Protoichthyosaurus.
facts.quote: a study published in 2017 by the British palaeontologist Dean R. Lomax and colleagues instead recovered Malawania as a basal thunnosaur, with Ichthyosaurus forming the sister taxon of Protoichthyosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2025, Lomax and colleagues recovered Malawania within the Ichthyosauridae as part of a clade containing all recognized members of the family.
facts.quote: In 2025, when describing the leptonectid Xiphodracon, Lomax and colleagues once again recovered Malawania within the Ichthyosauridae, this time as part of a clade comprising all currently recognised members of the family.
